learn.intro: Good history starts with a good question. This topic shows you how to turn a simple "when" question into a real enquiry, how sure we can be of a claim, and how historians explain why things happen, using Alphonse the Camel.

sections.title: 1. What makes a good historical question?

blocks.p: A factual question has one simple answer ("When did the UAE form?"). A historical enquiry asks "why", "how far" or "how significant", and needs evidence and judgement to answer.
Historians are honest about how sure they are. The certainty continuum runs: Certain → Very likely → Likely → Possible → Uncertain.
Qualifiers make your claims precise: "X was important" becomes "X was highly significant" or "X was somewhat significant". They show the strength of your argument.

evidence: Good enquiry stems: Why…? How far…? How significant…? How certain…?
Certainty continuum: certain → very likely → likely → possible → uncertain.

sections.title: 2. Cause and consequence: Alphonse the Camel

blocks.p: Alphonse the Camel is loaded with more and more until one final straw makes him collapse. The obvious answer is "the straw caused it". But would that straw have mattered without everything already loaded? The final straw is the trigger, not the most important cause.

ul: Long-term causes: building up over years.
Trigger: the immediate event that sets things off.
Underlying causes: the deeper conditions that made the event possible.

blocks.p: A consequence is a result of an event. Explaining connectives link causes to results: because, therefore, as a result, as a consequence, this meant that.
A real example: in 1066 the death of Edward the Confessor (January) triggered a crisis, but the deeper cause was that he had no children, leaving several rival claimants to the throne.

evidence: The trigger is not always the most important cause.
Edward the Confessor died in January 1066 without children.

misconceptions.wrong: The last thing that happened is the most important cause.
misconceptions.right: The trigger is often the least important. Long-term causes usually matter more.
Most events have several causes that work together.

misconceptions.wrong: "Why" and "when" questions are equally good enquiries.
misconceptions.right: "When" questions have one answer. "Why" and "how far" questions need evidence and judgement.

evidence.q: Using Alphonse the Camel, explain why the final event is not necessarily the most important cause.
evidence.model: The final straw only made Alphonse collapse because he was already carrying a huge load. Without everything else, the straw would not have mattered, so it was the trigger, not the most important cause.

evidence.q: Improve this claim using a qualifier and a reason: "Oil was important for Dubai."
evidence.model: The discovery of oil in 1966 was highly significant for Dubai because it provided money to build infrastructure, which meant the city could grow much faster.

checklist.text: I can describe the difference between a factual question and an enquiry question.
I can describe long-term, short-term and trigger causes.
I can explain why the trigger is not always the most important cause.
I can use explaining connectives to link causes and consequences.
I can use qualifiers to show how certain or how significant something is.
I can judge which cause was most important and justify it.

questions.label: Teacher-created practice question
questions.q: "The final event is always the most important cause." How far do you agree? Use Alphonse the Camel and the events of 1066 in your answer.
questions.asks: Judge whether triggers matter most, using both the Alphonse model and a real example.
steps: Explain what a trigger is, using Alphonse.
Explain a deeper cause (e.g. Edward having no children).
Weigh them using qualifiers and reach a judgement.
questions.plan: 2 minutes planning, 9 minutes writing, 1 minute checking connectives.
mistakes: Retelling the Alphonse story without explaining

model.t: I largely disagree, because the final event is usually only the trigger.

Alphonse only collapsed under the final straw because he was already carrying a huge load. Similarly, Edward the Confessor's death in January 1066 triggered a crisis, but the deeper cause was that he had no children.
model.n: E: model plus precise historical evidence.

model.t: This meant several claimants believed they had a right to the throne, so a crisis was likely whenever Edward died.
Therefore the long-term cause was more important than the trigger.

full: P: I agree / disagree to a large / some extent…
J: Overall, the most important cause was… because…
some: P: qualified claim (highly / partly / to some extent…)
E: precise evidence (name, date, number, source)
E: explain with a connective (because / this meant that / therefore)
J: judgement that answers the question

steps: Use a different enquiry stem for each.

stretch.task: Can a question ever be too uncertain to be worth asking? Explain with an example.
Which cause was necessary, rather than simply important? What is the difference?

If Edward the Confessor had had a son, would 1066 still have been a crisis? Explain your reasoning.
